extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of theology and religious apologetics; those evaluating claims about miracles, prophecy, and Christian evidences
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Pascal's criteria for judging miracles, prophecies, apostolic testimony, and related proofs used in Christian apologetics. Focus is on the standards, tests, and explanatory notes Pascal gives for distinguishing true from false miracles and for assessing religious claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual test of doctrine and miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles enable us to judge of doctrine, and doctrine enables us to judge of miracles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rule for distinguishing true from false miracles must preserve the evidential force of true miracles; neither miracles nor doctrine alone should be made useless by the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaic rules for judging prophets/miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: Moses gave two rules: that the prediction does not come to pass (Deut. xviii) and that they do not lead to idolatry (Deut. xiii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two negative tests are offered as classical criteria to detect false prophets and false miracles; Pascal cites them as part of the biblical standard for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of miracle
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is an effect which exceeds the natural power of the means which are employed for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect does not exceed the natural power of the means (e.g., healing by invocation of the devil), it is not a true miracle; precision about the natural powers involved is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of inward and outward supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two fundamentals, one inward (grace) and the other outward (miracles); both are supernatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both kinds of supernatural phenomena matter for assessing religion: inward conversion/grace and outward signs/miracles must be considered together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles necessary to convince whole man
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles and truth are necessary, because it is necessary to convince the entire man, in body and soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miracles address the bodily/sensory aspect of belief while doctrine addresses the mind; both functions contribute to full conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of false miracles implies some true ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The abundance of false miracles, revelations, and religions does not disprove true miracles; rather, the existence of true instances explains why many false ones are believed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: because some remedies are true, many false remedies are believed; similarly for miracles and religions. Prevalence of false claims is not a disproof of the real phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence criterion for miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: The second miracle can suppose the first, but the first cannot suppose the second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is an order or dependency among miraculous signs; some miracles presuppose others and an evidential sequence matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a rule to judge miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: If there were no rule to judge of miracles, miracles would be useless; hence a strict but fair rule is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgment must be strict to exclude falsehoods but just enough to allow true exceptions; the existence of exceptions requires careful application of a rule rather than wholesale skepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disposition shapes reception of miracles
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes people not believe true miracles is lack of love; what makes people believe false miracles is also rooted in moral/psychological disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The believer's or unbeliever's heart (love, desire, predisposition) influences whether they accept or reject miraculous evidence; epistemic judgments are not purely intellectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles suffice when doctrine is consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: When doctrine is not inconsistent with the miracles, miracles can suffice as proof; miracles can override ambiguities in prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where prophecies are obscure or ambiguous, clear miraculous evidence can provide decisive confirmation, provided the doctrine is not incompatible with the signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles historically make unbelief culpable
rubrics_metrics.description: Had there been no miracles, there would have been no sin in not believing; miracles render refusal culpable by providing clearer evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miracles raise the standard of evidence and thereby responsibility; historical miracles thus affect moral accountability for unbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostolic testimony credibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: The apostles' testimony is unlikely to be a collusive deception because they risked prisons, tortures, and death; either they were deceived or deceivers, and both hypotheses are problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider motives, risks, and the implausibility of a mass persistent lie when evaluating apostolic claims of resurrection appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial moderation as evidence of authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The moderation and lack of invective in the Gospel writers (no invectives against persecutors) is evidence of natural disinterestedness and supports authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traits such as not flattering followers or attacking enemies gratuitously suggest the writers were not inventing for gain; style and impartiality are evidential features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection-by-enemies as evidential sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The Jews' rejection of Christ functions as proof: whether they received or rejected Him, their attitude provides testimony; their rejection fulfilled prophecies and makes them 'irreproachable witnesses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that opponents would not accept Jesus and yet could not show prophecy contradiction is taken as confirming the prophetic design; hostile behavior can be evidence when it fulfills predicted patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles must not promote idolatry
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign is suspect if it leads people to idolatry; one of the Mosaic tests is that true miracles should not lead to idolatrous worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even spectacular effects are disqualified if their consequence is to draw worship away from God; ethical and theological outcomes of signs matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment must account for differing dispensations
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be different rules in different times (distinction of the times): one rule during Moses' time, another in the present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections that appeal to temporal differences must be considered; criteria for miracles and prophets are not necessarily uniform across historical dispensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical pattern: miracles on side of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: In disputes about the true God and the truth of religion, historically miracles have not appeared on the side of error but on the side of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal adduces biblical examples (Elijah vs false prophets, Jeremiah vs Hananiah, etc.) as an historical pattern to weigh as part of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with ambiguous uses of the word 'miracle'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'miracle' (portentum, miraculum) is used in different senses in Scripture (fear, portent, simulacrum), so lexical ambiguity must be cleared when using miracle as a test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exegetical attention is required: do not treat every scriptural 'miracle' reference as the same kind of proof; context and original language matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: False miracles exploit the mind's inability to isolate true particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: People are prone to generalize from some true instances to accept many false instances because they cannot distinguish which particular effects are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should be cautious about overgeneralizing from authentic instances; demand specific corroboration rather than relying on an inference from possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles can be used both to convert and to condemn
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracles do not simply convert; they can also serve to condemn those who resist evident signs (Pascal notes 'Miracles serve not to convert, but to condemn' as a paradoxical judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the rhetorical and moral function of miraculous signs in context: signs may vindicate truth but also expose and condemn hardness of heart.
